title: Latency, Throughput & Cost Trade-offs
interviewAnswer: Latency is time per request; throughput is work per unit time. Batching usually improves throughput/GPU utilization but can increase individual-request latency, so tune around the product SLO and cost.
why: System-design interviews test whether you can reason about service quality and cost, not only model accuracy.
intuition: Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how much work the system completes per unit time. Batching can improve throughput but may add waiting latency.
deepDive: Average latency hides tail behavior, so track p50/p95/p99. Throughput is bounded by compute, memory bandwidth, I/O and queueing. Increasing batch size often improves GPU utilization until memory or tail-latency limits. Concurrency can raise throughput but cause contention. Autoscaling needs a metric tied to bottlenecks—queue depth, GPU utilization or requests per replica—not arbitrary CPU alone.
math:
Throughput ≈ completed requests / time
Little’s Law (stable system): L = λW, relating average items in system, arrival rate and time in system.
workedExample: An LLM endpoint can batch 16 prompts for high token throughput, but an interactive chat may prefer smaller dynamic batches to keep first-token latency low.
commonMistakes: Optimizing mean latency instead of tail latency.
Equating more replicas with linear throughput scaling.
Ignoring queueing time and model-loading cold starts.
followUps: How do you choose an autoscaling signal?
What is the cost/latency trade-off of larger models?
production: Set explicit SLOs and cost budgets, profile the bottleneck, load-test realistic traffic and monitor queue depth, utilization, tail latency and error rate together.
